<reason>CON (A) built the more concrete causal mechanism: a cap doesn't eliminate liquidity demand, it reroutes marginal borrowers toward payday, title, and pawn markets that already sit beside today's uncapped cards. CON pressed this by exploiting PRO's own concession that capped-card borrowers "will make the minimum" — showing PRO's harm-reduction story reduces to "cheaper revolving debt for survivors" while saying nothing about where excluded borrowers actually land. PRO's strongest counter-move was the burden-shift ("I don't have to prove they land safer, you have to prove they land worse") and the sharp Q1 pressure question asking whether CON's logic forbids any cap whenever a worse market exists. CON's answer to that question (distinguishing this cap from a hypothetical cap paired with alternatives) was serviceable but somewhat conclusory, costing CON some ground. Still, across the debate PRO never supplied an affirmative account of where displaced borrowers go besides asserting the migration is "unproven," while CON kept the substitution channel as a live, unrebutted mechanism. PRO's moral framing ("quiet confiscation," "millstone," "tax on desperation") was vivid and helped crystallize stakes, but rhetorical framing didn't resolve the empirical gap CON exploited. A's case suffered a real execution cost from two clipped turns (opening and closing), which trims the margin, but the substantive architecture of CON's argument was stronger and more consistently defended across rounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's [A2.1]-[A2.2], which used PRO's own admission that capped-card borrowers "will make the minimum" to collapse PRO's harm-reduction narrative into a distinction without a difference, combined with A's refusal in Rebuttal 2 to accept the burden-shift PRO proposed in the Pressure Questions round.</best_rebuttal>
